title: Bragg and Bragg, 'The reflection of X-rays by crystals' (1913)
summary: William Henry Bragg and William Lawrence Bragg published in Proceedings of the Royal Society of London, Series A, in July 1913 a study of X-rays reflected from planes within a crystal, measured with a spectrometer-like apparatus in which an ionisation chamber replaced the telescope. The abstract reports a reflected pencil from mica's cleavage plane strong enough to impress a photographic plate in a few minutes' exposure.
body: William Henry Bragg and William Lawrence Bragg published "The reflection of X-rays by crystals" in Proceedings of the Royal Society of London. Series A, volume 88, issue 605, pages 428–438, dated 1 July 1913. The abstract states that in a discussion of the Laue photographs it has been shown that they "may conveniently be interpreted as due to the reflection of X-rays in such planes within the crystal as are rich in atoms", which it says leads to the attempt to use cleavage planes as mirrors. It reports that mica "gives a reflected pencil from its cleavage plane strong enough to make a visible impression on a photographic plate in a few minutes’ exposure", and that the reflected pencil can also be detected by the ionisation method. For closer examination the authors used "an apparatus resembling a spectrometer in form, an ionisation chamber taking the place of the telescope", the chamber being tubular, 15 cm long and 5 cm in diameter and filled with sulphur dioxide to increase the ionisation current.
